sections.text: Ownership is how Rust manages memory without a garbage collector and without you freeing memory by hand. It rests on three rules.
1. Every value has one owner, a variable. 2. There is only one owner at a time. 3. When the owner goes out of scope, the value is dropped (its memory is freed).
A String stores its text on the heap. When you assign it to another variable, ownership moves. The old variable can't be used any more:
Passing a value to a function moves it too, unless the function hands it back:
Think of it like handing someone a physical book. Once you've given it away, you don't have it any more. That's how Rust knows exactly when it's safe to free memory.

A move is a cheap shallow copy of the pointer, length and capacity; the heap data isn't copied. Because only one owner exists, there's no double free and no need for reference counting. C++ programmers: this is like std::move, but checked by the compiler and the default.

exercise.prompt:
The program uses name after it was moved into greet. Change greet so it doesn't need to own the String: make the parameter a reference (&String) and call it with &name. It should print: Hello, Ferris
Bye, Ferris

quiz.question: How many owners can a value have at one time?
What happens to a value when its owner goes out of scope?
options: It's dropped and its memory freed
It stays until the program ends

quiz.question: After let b = a; where a is a String, can you still use a?
